title: Gradient boosting
story:
Averaging fixes instability and cannot fix a mistake everyone makes. Grow a thousand trees independently on the same problem and each is fitted to the same target; whatever they all get wrong in the same direction survives the average untouched. To attack that you have to stop fitting them independently.

Boosting does the obvious thing once you say it out loud: fit a model, look at what it got wrong, and fit the next model to that. Repeat. Each stage is deliberately concerned with the part the ensemble has so far failed on, so the errors the sequence corrects are the shared ones rather than the idiosyncratic ones.

Friedman's contribution in 2001 was to say precisely what "what it got wrong" should mean, and the framing is the part worth carrying. He views function estimation from the perspective of numerical optimisation in function space rather than parameter space, connecting stagewise additive expansions with steepest-descent minimisation. Read that carefully: the object being optimised is the function itself, the step direction is the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, and each new tree is fitted to approximate that direction. Which means the method is not tied to squared error at all — it is a general gradient descent boosting paradigm for additive expansions based on any fitting criterion, and the paper gives algorithms for least squares, least absolute deviation and Huber loss in regression and for the multiclass logistic likelihood in classification. Residual-fitting is what it looks like in the special case where the loss is squared error, which is why that special case is how everyone first learns it.

The consequence is the mirror image of the previous lesson and it is the single most important thing to know about boosting. Because each model is fitted to the state left by the ones before it, the models are not independent, the ensemble does not converge to a harmless limit, and adding stages eventually makes things worse. The number of stages is a genuine parameter that has to be chosen against held-out data, and it is controlled jointly with a learning rate that shrinks each stage's contribution — smaller steps, more of them.

The systems work matters more here than elsewhere because the sequence cannot be parallelised across stages. Chen and Guestrin's 2016 paper is about making the inner loop fast enough to be worth it: a sparsity-aware algorithm for sparse data, a weighted quantile sketch for approximate split finding, and results on cache access patterns, data compression and sharding that let the system scale beyond billions of examples with far fewer resources than existing systems. That engineering is why boosted trees, not forests, became the default for tabular problems.

problem.name: Stagewise additive modelling
problem.shape: An ensemble of independently fitted models has stopped improving, and what remains is error they all share rather than error that averages away.
tell: averaging more models has stopped helping
the data is tabular and a strong baseline is wanted
training and held-out error are both still falling
problem.move: Fit models in sequence, each to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions, and shrink each contribution by a learning rate so that progress is made in many small steps. Choose the number of stages against held-out data rather than increasing it freely, and pick the loss deliberately, because the method accepts any differentiable criterion.
problem.invariant: Each stage performs one step of steepest descent in the space of functions, with the new model approximating the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions. Fitting to residuals is the special case where that loss is squared error.
problem.breaks: The sequential dependence that makes boosting powerful removes the protection a forest has. The models are not independent samples of anything, so the ensemble does not converge to a limit — continuing to add stages drives training error down and held-out error back up, which makes the stage count a parameter requiring validation rather than a budget.

cost.time: the stages are inherently sequential and cannot be parallelised across, which is why the engineering of the inner loop determines whether the method is practical
cost.space: every stage is retained, as with a forest, and shallower trees are usual so the per-stage cost is lower
cost.beats: bagging, which cannot reduce shared bias however many models it averages, and a single model, which has no mechanism for correcting its own systematic error

worked.problem: What actually differs between averaging many trees and boosting them?
worked.reasoning:
Whether the models are fitted independently, and everything else follows from that one difference.

In a forest, each tree is grown on its own resample without reference to any other. The trees are independent draws from a distribution of models, the ensemble estimates the average of that distribution, and averaging reduces variance. What it cannot touch is bias: if every tree errs in the same direction, so does the average. This is why a forest's error converges to a limit as trees are added and why the tree count is a compute budget.

In boosting, each model is fitted to what the current ensemble has got wrong — specifically, to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the present predictions, which is steepest descent performed in function space rather than parameter space. Because each stage sees the state left by the previous ones, the models are not independent and the ensemble is not an average of anything. It is a sequence of correction steps, and correction steps attack exactly the shared error that averaging cannot.

The consequences diverge from there, and they are worth stating as a list because they are the practical content.

Overfitting. A forest converges; more trees do not hurt. A boosted ensemble does not converge in that way — keep adding stages and training error keeps falling while held-out error turns back up. So the stage count is a real hyper-parameter and needs validation, and it is chosen jointly with a learning rate that shrinks each step.

Parallelism. Forest trees are independent and can be grown simultaneously. Boosting stages depend on their predecessors and cannot be, which is why the engineering of the inner loop is decisive for whether the method is usable at scale.

Base model. Forests want strong, deep, low-bias trees, because the job is to average away their variance. Boosting wants weak, shallow ones, because the job is to accumulate many small corrections and a strong learner at each stage overshoots.

What bias-variance language captures, roughly, is that bagging is a variance reduction method and boosting is a bias reduction method. I would offer that as a summary rather than as the explanation, because the underlying fact is simpler and does more work: in one the models never see each other, and in the other each one is built to fix the last.

problem.practice: Fit a boosted model and plot both training and held-out error against the number of stages, far past the point of best held-out performance. Watch the two curves separate. Then halve the learning rate, refit, and find where the best stage count moved to.

beats.broke: Averaging independently grown models reduces their instability but cannot reduce error they all make in the same direction, because every one of them was fitted to the same target.
beats.fix: Fit the models in sequence, each to the negative gradient of the loss left by those before it — steepest descent carried out in the space of functions rather than the space of parameters, which makes the method work for any differentiable criterion.
beats.cost: The models are no longer independent, so the ensemble can be driven past usefulness by adding stages, and the number of stages becomes a parameter to be validated rather than a budget to be increased.

interview.q: What actually differs between averaging many trees and boosting them?
interview.trap: Answering only that one reduces variance and the other reduces bias. That is the consequence; the cause is that in one the models never see each other and in the other each is fitted to what the last got wrong, which is also why only one of the two can overfit by adding models.
interview.answer:
Whether the models are fitted independently. Everything else follows from that.

In a forest each tree is grown on its own resample without reference to the others, so the trees are independent draws from a distribution of models and the ensemble estimates that distribution's average. Averaging reduces variance and cannot touch bias: if every tree errs in the same direction, so does the average. Hence the error converges to a limit and the tree count is a compute budget.

In boosting each model is fitted to what the current ensemble got wrong — specifically to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the present predictions, which is steepest descent in function space rather than parameter space. Because each stage sees the state its predecessors left, the models are not independent and the ensemble is not an average. It is a sequence of corrections, and corrections attack precisely the shared error that averaging cannot.

The consequences diverge from there. Overfitting: a forest converges, while a boosted ensemble does not — keep adding stages and training error falls while held-out error turns back up, so the stage count is a real hyper-parameter chosen jointly with a learning rate. Parallelism: forest trees can be grown simultaneously, boosting stages cannot, which is why the engineering of the inner loop decides whether it is usable at scale. Base model: forests want deep low-bias trees to average variance away, boosting wants shallow ones because it accumulates many small corrections and a strong learner overshoots.

Summarising it as variance reduction against bias reduction is fair, but I would offer that as the consequence rather than the explanation — the underlying fact is simply that in one the models never see each other, and in the other each is built to fix the last.
